forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Merton's high-needs deficit was £69.1m at March 2026, with a further c.£23.3m rise forecast this year
news_drafts.lead:
Merton's deficit on the high needs part of its dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools and, in high needs, support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), "had grown to £69.1m" by 31 March 2026. A budget report to the Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Panel says the high needs budget has been in deficit since 2018/19. On the council's forecast for the first three months of the year, the deficit is estimated to rise by c.£23.3m in 2026/27.

The government will provide a High Needs Stability Grant for 90 per cent of historic high-needs deficits up to the end of 2025/26. That depends on approval of a SEND local reform plan, which Merton submitted to the Department for Education on 19 June 2026. The statutory override, the temporary rule that keeps such deficits off a council's main balance sheet, ends from 1 April 2028. The paper says the government will confirm further support for deficits arising in 2026-27 and 2027-28 before then. From 2028-29, it says, "SEND spending will be covered by the overall government DEL", meaning central government's departmental budget.

Merton's earmarked reserves are c.£123m, and the paper says c.£58.6m of that "should be available" against the deficit at 31 March 2026 if the grant is received. Any government non-compensation for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits will need to be met from these reserves. Its revenue reserves of c.£137m are the sixth highest among London's 32 boroughs.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 to Scrutiny - Budget report + Appendices (004)

news_drafts.headline: Merton's schools high-needs deficit reached £69.1m at March 2026, with £58.6m of reserves earmarked towards it
news_drafts.lead:
Merton's deficit on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, had grown to £69.1m by 31 March 2026. The council's budget report to the Children and Young People Overview and Scrutiny Panel estimates it will rise by about £23.3m during 2026/27.

The report says the government will provide a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90 per cent of historic high-needs deficits up to the end of 2025/26, subject to an approved special educational needs and disabilities local reform plan, which the council submitted on 19 June 2026. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, ends on 1 April 2028. Support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 "will not be unlimited", the report says.

Merton holds earmarked reserves of about £123m, of which about £58.6m is expected to be available towards the historic deficit, assuming the grant is received. The report says: "The extent to which the government do not compensate Merton for DSG deficits incurred in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will need to be met from this." Further detail on the reserves strategy will follow in future reports. The report shows Merton's revenue reserves of about £137m as the sixth highest among London's 32 boroughs.

news_drafts.headline: Merton Cabinet papers show £69.1m schools high needs deficit and £137m of revenue reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Merton's schools funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (known as high needs) has been in deficit since 2018/19 and had grown to £69.1m by 31 March 2026, according to budget papers for the Cabinet meeting on 19 October. The council says that is the second highest such deficit in London. It estimates a further £23.3m will build up in 2026/27.

The deficit sits on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The government's High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of the historic deficit. Ministers have indicated similar proportionate support may continue for deficits arising in 2026-27 and 2027-28, but confirmation is pending. From 2028-29, the papers say, spending on special needs will be covered by the government's overall departmental budget, so councils will no longer have to fund future costs from general funds once the statutory override (the temporary rule keeping such deficits off a council's main balance sheet) ends.

Merton held revenue reserves (money put aside) of about £137m at 31 March 2026, the sixth highest of London's 32 boroughs; the London average is £132m. Its capital reserves of £181m are third highest in Outer London. The papers say these figures put the council at low risk on the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy's Financial Resilience Index. About £58.6m of the earmarked reserves is intended to offset the historic schools deficit, conditional on the government grant. The papers state that if that support is not provided, the deficit would have to be met from general reserves.

findings.committee: South London Waste Partnership Joint Committee
findings.headline: SLWP reports a notable increase in contractor cost-cutting measures within its existing contracts
findings.detail: The paper says the increase in contractor cost-cutting is leading the SLWP data team to intensify contract performance management. It says the partnership must protect service quality and take a strong stance on these practices.
findings.matters: Contractor margin pressure on waste treatment contracts is a risk other councils and their lenders would want to see reported as a rising trend, not an isolated event.
findings.quote: There has also been a notable increase in contractor cost cutting measures within our existing contracts

findings.committee: South London Waste Partnership Joint Committee
findings.headline: The staffing budget assumes 3.5% inflation, against a 3.3% LGA pay award for 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper bases the 2027/28 staffing budget on 3.5% inflation, taken from the 3.3% LGA pay award for 2026/27. It says any actual 2027/28 increase will follow the LGA pay award for that year.
findings.matters: Pay assumptions in partnership budgets feed directly into the per-borough charge, so the gap between the budgeted and awarded rates matters to any council's staffing forecast.
findings.figures: 3.5% assumed staffing inflation; 3.3% LGA pay award 2026/27
findings.quote: The budgeted increase in overall staffing costs assumes 3.5% inflation

findings.committee: South London Waste Partnership Joint Committee
findings.headline: SLWP describes the residual-waste Emissions Trading Scheme exposure as "potentially significant" and says the ERF inclusion in the UK ETS has been delayed
findings.detail: The paper says extensive analysis of residual waste streams is under way to quantify ETS financial risk and to ensure boroughs pay only their true share. It says preparation continues even though the ERF inclusion has been delayed, so that cost risks can be identified and mitigated in time.
findings.matters: Any council with residual-waste contracts faces the same ETS cost question, and a finance director would need to know the exposure is being quantified while its scope is still changing.
findings.quote: quantify the potentially significant financial risk from the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS)

findings.committee: South London Waste Partnership Joint Committee
findings.headline: The paper states that the finance and business intelligence team was reduced in the 2025 staffing restructure, and that a 30% reduction in SLWP staff was made in April 2025
findings.detail: The paper says the leaner structure from April 2025 cut staff by 30%, and that the finance and BI team was reduced in that restructure while it takes on added data work. That work includes ETS residual-waste analysis, the Waste Watch project and contractor performance management.
findings.matters: A finance team reduced in size while taking on new statutory and data demands is a staffing pressure that other finance officers will recognise.
findings.quote: a leaner SLWP structure was put in place in April 2025 and the 30% reduction in staff delivered significant savings

findings.committee: South London Waste Partnership Joint Committee
findings.headline: The 2027/28 legal budget is estimated at £50,000, up from £30,000 last year, dependent on contractor discussions
findings.detail: The paper says the figure is an estimate that depends on the outcome of ongoing contractor discussions. It cites known legislative changes, including the Deposit Return Scheme, the Emissions Trading Scheme and Simpler Recycling, that may trigger those discussions, and says the timing is unknown.
findings.matters: Legal costs tied to contractor renegotiation are a cost many councils face as they adjust to new legislation, and this paper shows the estimate rising by two-thirds.
findings.quote: an estimated legal spend of £50,000, up from £30,000 last year

daily_post.lead: Temporary accommodation demand is one of the named cost pressures in the report, and the placement count and overspend are useful benchmarks for other councils facing the same homelessness trend.
